aimpl_batch.label: aimpl/4
aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Calculation of $\mathrm{TP}(\mathbb{Z})$ Fix a prime $p$. Let $j = \tau_{\geq 0} L_{K(1)} \mathbb{S}$. Then, $\mathrm{TP}(\mathbb{Z}_p) \simeq j^{tS^1}$, for the trivial $S^1$-action on $j$. Bokstedt and Madsen computed $\mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{Z})$, without calculating $\mathrm{TP}(\mathbb{Z})$. However, Hesselholt and Madsen calculated (in \cite{MR1317575}) $(L_{K(1)} \mathbb{S})^{tS^1}$. Their results suggest the following: Computations in algebraic K-theory Equivariant techniques in stable homotopy theory TP of the p-adic integers is equivalent to the Tate construction on the connective K(1)-local sphere.

aimpl_batch.label: aimpl/5
aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: $L$-theory of integers Equip $\mathrm{Pin}(2)$ (resp. $Q_8$) with the canonical $\mathbb{Z}/2$-action (resp. the action given by conjugation by $i$). Then, the $E_\infty$-map $L^s(\mathbb{Z})_{(2)} \to L^n(\mathbb{Z})$ can be identified by taking strict $\mathbb{Z}/2$-fixed points of the map $\mathbb{Z}_{(2)}^{t\mathrm{Pin}(2)} \to \mathbb{Z}^{tQ_8}$. (This map is induced by the inclusion $Q_8\subseteq \mathrm{Pin}(2)$.) The symmetric and normal $L$-theory of the integers was computed in \cite{arXiv:2004.06889}, and the Tate cohomology of $Q_8$ was computed by Atiyah in \cite{MR0148722}. The normal $L$-theory of $\mathbb{Z}$ looks very similar to the Tate cohomology of $Q_8$; similarly, the symmetric $L$-theory of $\mathbb{Z}$ looks very similar to the Tate cohomology of $\mathrm{Pin}(2)$.

oeis.label: A008486
oeis.text_excerpt: The conjecture is correct. Proof: For n=0 the theorem holds, the maximum planar graph has n+2=2 vertices and 1 edge. Now suppose that we have a connected planar graph with at least 3 vertices. If it contains a face that is not a triangle, we can add an edge that divides this face into two without breaking its planarity. Hence all maximum planar graphs are triangulations. Euler's formula for planar graphs states that in any planar simple graph with V vertices, E edges and F faces we have V+F-E=2. If all faces are triangles, then F=2E/3, which gives us E=3V-6. Hence for n>0 each maximum planar simple graph with n+2 vertices has 3n edges. - _Michal Forisek_, Apr 23 2009

aimpl_batch.label: aimpl/8
aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Quasi-convex subgroups Let $G$ be a hyperbolic free-by-cyclic group and $H$ a non-quasiconvex subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ contains a subgroup $F$ which is a virtual fibre or a virtual semi-fibre of a free-by-cyclic subgroup of $G$. A subgroup $F$ of a group $G$ is a \emph{semi-fibre} if there exists an injective non-surjective homomorphism $\varphi \colon F \to F$ such that $G$ is the HNN extension \[G = F \ast_{\varphi}.\] A subgroup $F$ of $G$ is a \emph{virtual semi-fibre} if there exists a finite index subgroup $G'$ of $G$ such that $F$ is a semi-fibre of $G'$. Subgroups of free-by-cyclic groups Rigidity properties of free-by-cyclic groups Every non-quasiconvex subgroup of a hyperbolic free-by-cyclic group contains an appropriate virtual fibre or semi-fibre.

oeis.text_excerpt: The simple algorithm of taking the first C (or [n/2] if less) persons up to their destination, then the last C persons down to their destination, and if not finished, starting over with floor C+1 as new ground floor with n' = n - 2C, yields an upper bound a(n) <= 2n - 2 + C + a(n - 2C) for n > 2C + 1. aimpl_batch.label: aimpl/23
aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Distinct distances and related problems (1) Let $S\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three points collinear. Then $S$ determines at least $|S|/2$ distinct distances. (2) Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three collinear. Then one can remove $O(1)$-many points so that the number of isosceles triangles is at most $1.99\binom{n}{2}$. (3) Given a set $S$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three collinear. Then $S$ determines $\Omega(n^2)$ perpendicular bisectors containing at most 1 point of $S$ each, unless $S$ is the vertices of a regular polygon together with its center. Discrete geometry High-dimensional phenomena in discrete analysis After deleting only O(1) points from any n-point planar set in general position, the remaining number of isosceles triangles is at most 1.99 times n

aimpl_batch.label: aimpl/22
aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Equi-isoclinic subspaces Let $N_\alpha^k(d)$ be the maximum number of $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^d$, every pair of which is equi-isoclinic with angle $\alpha$. Then (1) $N_{\alpha}^k(d)=O_{\alpha,k}(d)$. (2) $N_{\alpha}^k(d)=O_{k}(d)+o_{\alpha,k}(d)$. Given $k$-dimensional linear subspaces $U,V\leq \mathbb{R}^d$, we say that $U,V$ are equi-isoclinic with angle $\alpha$ if every unit vector in $U$ projects down onto $V$ a vector of length $\alpha$. Discrete geometry High-dimensional phenomena in discrete analysis For fixed angle and dimension k, the maximum size of an equi-isoclinic k-subspace family grows at most linearly in d.

aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: $L$-theory of integers Equip $\mathrm{Pin}(2)$ (resp. $Q_8$) with the canonical $\mathbb{Z}/2$-action (resp. the action given by conjugation by $i$). Then, the $E_\infty$-map $L^s(\mathbb{Z})_{(2)} \to L^n(\mathbb{Z})$ can be identified by taking strict $\mathbb{Z}/2$-fixed points of the map $\mathbb{Z}_{(2)}^{t\mathrm{Pin}(2)} \to \mathbb{Z}^{tQ_8}$. (This map is induced by the inclusion $Q_8\subseteq \mathrm{Pin}(2)$.) The symmetric and normal $L$-theory of the integers was computed in \cite{arXiv:2004.06889}, and the Tate cohomology of $Q_8$ was computed by Atiyah in \cite{MR0148722}. The normal $L$-theory of $\mathbb{Z}$ looks very similar to the Tate cohomology of $Q_8$; similarly, the symmetric $L$-theory of $\mathbb{Z}$ looks very similar to the Tate cohomology of $\mathrm{Pin}(2)$.

aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: $\pi(C_5^3)=2\sqrt3-3$ Mubayi and R\"odl~\cite{mubayi+rodl:02} have given bounds on $\pi(C_5^3)$, where $C_5^3$ is the tight $3$-graph $5$-cycle: $$ C_5^3=\{123,234,345,451,512\}. $$ In particular, the lower bound $\pi(C_5^3)\ge 2\sqrt3-3$ comes from the following construction: partition the vertex set into two parts $A$ and $B$, take all triples that intersect $A$ precisely in $2$ vertices, and recursively repeat this construction within $B$. Finding the optimal ratio between $|A|$ and $|B|$ gives the required. Razborov's~\cite{razborov:10} flag algebra computations showed that $\pi(C_5^3) < 0.4683$ (note that $2\sqrt3-3=0.4641...$). This makes the following conjecture plausible. Tight $5$-Cycle Hypergraph Turán problem The tight 3-uniform 5-cycle has Turan density 2 sqrt(3)-3.

aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Distinct distances and related problems (1) Let $S\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three points collinear. Then $S$ determines at least $|S|/2$ distinct distances. (2) Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three collinear. Then one can remove $O(1)$-many points so that the number of isosceles triangles is at most $1.99\binom{n}{2}$. (3) Given a set $S$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three collinear. Then $S$ determines $\Omega(n^2)$ perpendicular bisectors containing at most 1 point of $S$ each, unless $S$ is the vertices of a regular polygon together with its center. Quasi-convex subgroups
Let $G$ be a hyperbolic free-by-cyclic group and $H$ a non-quasiconvex subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ contains a subgroup $F$ which is a virtual fibre or a virtual semi-fibre of a free-by-cyclic subgroup of $G$.
A subgroup $F$ of a group $G$ is a \emph{semi-fibre} if there exists an injective non-surjective homomorphism $\varphi \colon F \to F$ such that $G$ is the HNN extension \[G = F \ast_{\varphi}.\] A subgroup $F$ of $G$ is a \emph{virtual semi-fibre} if there exists a finite index subgroup $G'$ of $G$ such that $F$ is a semi-fibre of $G'$.
Subgroups of free-by-cyclic groups

Every non-quasiconvex subgroup of a hyperbolic free-by-cyclic group contains an appropriate virtual fibre or semi-fibre.

aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Let $F = F(a,b,c,d,e)$ be a free group of rank five. For example, take n = 2. Then the options are a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4 = 1 or 3; one can change the sign of any of the a_i's and get 1; or -a_1-a_2+a_3+a_4 = 1. oeis.text_excerpt: The conjecture is correct. Proof: For n=0 the theorem holds, the maximum planar graph has n+2=2 vertices and 1 edge. Now suppose that we have a connected planar graph with at least 3 vertices. If it contains a face that is not a triangle, we can add an edge that divides this face into two without breaking its planarity. Hence all maximum planar graphs are triangulations. Euler's formula for planar graphs states that in any planar simple graph with V vertices, E edges and F faces we have V+F-E=2. If all faces are triangles, then F=2E/3, which gives us E=3V-6. Hence for n>0 each maximum planar simple graph with n+2 vertices has 3n edges. - _Michal Forisek_, Apr 23 2009

oeis.label: A008486
oeis.text_excerpt: The conjecture is correct. Proof: For n=0 the theorem holds, the maximum planar graph has n+2=2 vertices and 1 edge. Now suppose that we have a connected planar graph with at least 3 vertices. If it contains a face that is not a triangle, we can add an edge that divides this face into two without breaking its planarity. Hence all maximum planar graphs are triangulations. Euler's formula for planar graphs states that in any planar simple graph with V vertices, E edges and F faces we have V+F-E=2. If all faces are triangles, then F=2E/3, which gives us E=3V-6. Hence for n>0 each maximum planar simple graph with n+2 vertices has 3n edges. - _Michal Forisek_, Apr 23 2009

aimpl_batch.label: aimpl/8
aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Quasi-convex subgroups Let $G$ be a hyperbolic free-by-cyclic group and $H$ a non-quasiconvex subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ contains a subgroup $F$ which is a virtual fibre or a virtual semi-fibre of a free-by-cyclic subgroup of $G$. A subgroup $F$ of a group $G$ is a \emph{semi-fibre} if there exists an injective non-surjective homomorphism $\varphi \colon F \to F$ such that $G$ is the HNN extension \[G = F \ast_{\varphi}.\] A subgroup $F$ of $G$ is a \emph{virtual semi-fibre} if there exists a finite index subgroup $G'$ of $G$ such that $F$ is a semi-fibre of $G'$. Subgroups of free-by-cyclic groups Rigidity properties of free-by-cyclic groups Every non-quasiconvex subgroup of a hyperbolic free-by-cyclic group contains an appropriate virtual fibre or semi-fibre.

oeis.label: A333715
oeis.text_excerpt: For fixed m = 1,2,3,..., we conjecture that the sequence b(n) := a(m*n) satisfies a recurrence of the form P(6*m,n)*b(n+1) + P(6*m,-n)*b(n-1) = Q(3*m,n^2)*b(n), where the polynomials P(6*m,n) and Q(3*m,n^2) have degree 6*m. Conjecturally, the 6*m zeros of the polynomial Q(3*m,n^2) belong to the interval [-1, 1] and 6*m - 4 of these zeros appear to be approximated by the rational numbers +- k/(4*m), where 1 <= k <= 4*m - 3, k not a multiple of 4.

oeis.label: A103885
oeis.text_excerpt: More generally, for fixed m = 1,2,3,..., we conjecture that the sequence b(n) := a(m*n) satisfies a recurrence of the form ( Product_{k = 1..2*m} (2*m*n + k) ) * P(2*m,n)*b(n+1) + (-1)^m*( Product_{k = 1..2*m} (2*m*n - k) ) * P(2*m,-n)*b(n-1) = Q(2*m,n^2)*b(n), where the polynomials P(2*m,n) and Q(2*m,n) have degree 2*m. Conjecturally, the polynomial P(2*m,n) = P(2*m,1-n) and has real zeros in the interval [0, 1]. The 4*m zeros of the polynomial Q(2*m,n^2) seem to belong to the interval [-1, 1] and 4*m - 2 of these zeros appear to be approximated by the rational numbers +- k/(3*m), where 1 <= k <= 3*m - 2, k not a multiple of 3. (End)

oeis.label: A002003
oeis.text_excerpt: For fixed m = 1,2,3,..., we conjecture that the sequence b(n) := a(m*n) satisfies a recurrence of the form P(2*m,n)*b(n+1) + P(2*m,-n)*b(n-1) = Q(2*m,n)*b(n), where the polynomials P(2*m,n) and Q(2*m,n) have degree 2*m. Conjecturally, the polynomial Q(2*m,n) is an even function of n; its 2*m zeros seem to belong to the interval [-1, 1] and 2*m - 2 of these zeros appear to lie close to the rational numbers of the form +-(2*k + 1)/(2*m), where 0 <= k <= m - 2. Cf. A103885. (End)

oeis.label: A014442
oeis.text_excerpt: The conjecture is true. If p is a Pythagorean prime, -1 is a quadratic residue mod p. Then -1 has exactly two square roots mod p, i.e., there are exactly two integers x,y with 1 <= x,y <= p-1 such that x^2 == y^2 == -1 (mod p), i.e., p divides x^2 + 1 and y^2 + 1, and moreover y == -x (mod p) so x + y = p, and x*y == -x^2 == 1 (mod p). Any other prime factor q of x^2 + 1 must divide (x^2 + 1)/p, and since x^2+1 < p^2 we have q < p, so a(x) = p and similarly a(y) = p. - _Robert Israel_, Jun 11 2015

Conjecturally, the 6*m zeros of the polynomial Q(3*m,n^2) belong to the interval [-1, 1] and 6*m - 4 of these zeros appear to be approximated by the rational numbers +- k/(4*m), where 1 <= k <= 4*m - 3, k not a multiple of 4.

oeis.label: A103885

Conjecturally, the polynomial P(2*m,n) = P(2*m,1-n) and has real zeros in the interval [0, 1]. $\pi(C_5^3)=2\sqrt3-3$
Mubayi and R\"odl~\cite{mubayi+rodl:02} have given bounds on $\pi(C_5^3)$, where $C_5^3$ is the tight $3$-graph $5$-cycle: $$ C_5^3=\{123,234,345,451,512\}. $$ In particular, the lower bound $\pi(C_5^3)\ge 2\sqrt3-3$ comes from the following construction: partition the vertex set into two parts $A$ and $B$, take all triples that intersect $A$ precisely in $2$ vertices, and recursively repeat this construction within $B$. Finding the optimal ratio between $|A|$ and $|B|$ gives the required. Razborov's~\cite{razborov:10} flag algebra computations showed that $\pi(C_5^3) < 0.4683$ (note that $2\sqrt3-3=0.4641...$). This makes the following conjecture plausible.
Tight $5$-Cycle
Hypergraph Turán problem
The tight 3-uniform 5-cycle has Turan density 2 sqrt(3)-3.

Each star is triangle-free (any two non-center vertices share no edge within the star), and their union covers all edges of `⊤`. **Proof sketch (star triangle-free):** If `{a, b, c}` were a triangle in `H_m`, then each of the three edges `{a, b}`, `{a, c}`, `{b, c}` would pass through `m`. oeis.text_excerpt: The conjecture is correct. Proof: For n=0 the theorem holds, the maximum planar graph has n+2=2 vertices and 1 edge. Now suppose that we have a connected planar graph with at least 3 vertices. If it contains a face that is not a triangle, we can add an edge that divides this face into two without breaking its planarity. Hence all maximum planar graphs are triangulations. Euler's formula for planar graphs states that in any planar simple graph with V vertices, E edges and F faces we have V+F-E=2. If all faces are triangles, then F=2E/3, which gives us E=3V-6. Hence for n>0 each maximum planar simple graph with n+2 vertices has 3n edges. - _Michal Forisek_, Apr 23 2009

oeis.label: A008486
oeis.text_excerpt: The conjecture is correct. Proof: For n=0 the theorem holds, the maximum planar graph has n+2=2 vertices and 1 edge. Now suppose that we have a connected planar graph with at least 3 vertices. If it contains a face that is not a triangle, we can add an edge that divides this face into two without breaking its planarity. Hence all maximum planar graphs are triangulations. Euler's formula for planar graphs states that in any planar simple graph with V vertices, E edges and F faces we have V+F-E=2. If all faces are triangles, then F=2E/3, which gives us E=3V-6. Hence for n>0 each maximum planar simple graph with n+2 vertices has 3n edges. - _Michal Forisek_, Apr 23 2009

Monotonicity of the spectral gap
For a bounded convex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, the spectral gap $\lambda_2(\Omega, \alpha)-\lambda_1(\Omega, \alpha)$ is strictly increasing as a function of $\alpha>0$. In particular, the Neumann gap provides a lower bound for the Dirichlet gap: $$ \mu_1(\Omega) < \lambda_2(\Omega)-\lambda_1(\Omega). $$
The conjecture was originally formulated by R. Smits \cite{MR1381604}. The following formulation can be found in a recent preprint by R. Laugesen \cite{arXiv:1905.07658}.
The Robin Laplacian
Shape optimization with surface interactions

Discrete Bareket's conjecture
Among all triangles of a given area $\lambda_1(\Omega, \alpha)$ is: \begin{enumerate} \item minimized by the equilateral triangle when $\alpha>0$. \item maximized by the equilateral triangle when $\alpha < 0$. \end{enumerate}
In the same spirit as Bareket's conjecture one can ask what polygon maximizes $\lambda_1(\Omega, \alpha)$, $\alpha < 0$, among all polygons of the same area and having no more than $N$ sides. Similarly, one can ask the corresponding question when $\alpha>0$ in which case the problem is to minimize the eigenvalue. The following conjecture concerns the case $N = 3$.
The Robin Laplacian

Among equal-area triangles and positive Robin parameter, the equilateral triangle minimizes the lowest Robin eigenvalue.

Bareket \cite{MR430552}, it was conjectured that the lowest Robin eigenvalue $\lambda_1(\Omega,\alpha)$ on a bounded domain $\Omega$ with a boundary parameter $\alpha < 0$ is maximized by the ball among all sets of equal measure. In particular, the Neumann gap provides a lower bound for the Dirichlet gap: $$ \mu_1(\Omega) < \lambda_2(\Omega)-\lambda_1(\Omega). $$ The conjecture was originally formulated by R. Smits \cite{MR1381604}. The following formulation can be found in a recent preprint by R. Laugesen \cite{arXiv:1905.07658}. aimpl_batch.label: aimpl/53
aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Hot spots conjecture The first non-trivial Neumann eigenfunction does not have global extrema in the interior of $\Omega$ if \begin{enumerate} \item $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is simply connected. \item $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \ge 3$) is convex. \end{enumerate} This conjecture is often attributed to J. Rauch, who has formulated it in terms of large-time behaviuor of the heat semigroup generated by the Neumann Laplacian. On the qualitative level, this conjecture manifests as follows: for an insulated flat piece of metal with an arbitrary initial temperature distribution, given enough time, the hottest point on the metal will lie on its boundary. Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bouned convex domain and let $u$ be the principal eigenfunction of the Dirichlet Laplacian on $\Omega$. By a classical result of H. Brascamp and E. Lieb $u$ is log-concave \cite{MR0450480}. Moreover, it is known that $u$ is power-concave meaning that $u^\alpha$ is concave in the usual sense for certain powers $\alpha > 0$. The best concavity exponent for a domain $\Omega$ is defined as \[ \alpha(\Omega) :=\sup\{\alpha \ge 0\colon u^\alpha \mbox{ is concave}\}. \] The following conjecture was formulated in \cite{MR1280948} by P. oeis.text_excerpt: For n > 250 the terms are concentrated along seven lines, see the linked images. Concavity of the principal Dirichlet eigenfunction
The best concavity exponent $\alpha(\Omega)$ is maximized by the ball.
Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bouned convex domain and let $u$ be the principal eigenfunction of the Dirichlet Laplacian on $\Omega$. By a classical result of H. Brascamp and E. Lieb $u$ is log-concave \cite{MR0450480}. Moreover, it is known that $u$ is power-concave meaning that $u^\alpha$ is concave in the usual sense for certain powers $\alpha > 0$. The best concavity exponent for a domain $\Omega$ is defined as \[ \alpha(\Omega) :=\sup\{\alpha \ge 0\colon u^\alpha \mbox{ is concave}\}. \] The following conjecture was formulated in \cite{MR1280948} by P. Lindqvist.

oeis.label: A092287
oeis.text_excerpt: Conjecture: Let p be a prime and let ordp(n,p) denote the exponent of the highest power of p that divides n. For example, ordp(48,2)=4, since 48=3*(2^4). Then we conjecture that the prime factorization of a(n) is given by the formula: ordp(a(n),p) = (floor(n/p))^2 + (floor(n/p^2))^2 + (floor(n/p^3))^2 + .... Compare this to the de Polignac-Legendre formula for the prime factorization of n!: ordp(n!,p) = floor(n/p) + floor(n/p^2) + floor(n/p^3) + .... This suggests that a(n) can be considered as generalization of n!. See A129453 for the analog for a(n) of Pascal's triangle. See A129454 for the sequence defined as a triple product of gcd(i,j,k). - _Peter Bala_, Apr 16 2007

The first non-trivial Neumann eigenfunction does not have global extrema in the interior of $\Omega$ if \begin{enumerate} \item $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is simply connected. \item $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \ge 3$) is convex. \end{enumerate}
This conjecture is often attributed to J. Rauch, who has formulated it in terms of large-time behaviuor of the heat semigroup generated by the Neumann Laplacian. On the qualitative level, this conjecture manifests as follows: for an insulated flat piece of metal with an arbitrary initial temperature distribution, given enough time, the hottest point on the metal will lie on its boundary.

Log-Brunn-Minkowski Inequality
Show that if $K$ and $L$ symmetric convex bodies in $\R^n$, then for all $0 \leq t \leq 1$ the following hods $$ |tK +_\circ (1-t)L| \geq |K|^t |L|^{1-t} $$ with equality if and only if $K = L$ or $K$ and $L$ are parallelograms with parallel sides.
For convex bodies $K$ and $L$ in $\R^n$ with support functions $h_K$ and $h_L$ the logarithmic sum $tK +_\circ (1-t)L$ is defined as $$ tK +_\circ (1-t)L = \underset{u \in S^{n-1}}{\cap} \left\{x \in \R^n:\ \langle x, u\rangle \leq h_K(u)^th_L(u)^{1-t} \right\} $$ where $h_K(u) = \max\limits_{x \in K} \langle x, u\rangle .$
Inequalities
Symmetry and convexity in geometric inequalities
The intended claim is the origin-symmetric log-Brunn-Minkowski inequality.

$L_p$-Brunn Minkowski inequality
Show that if $K$ and $L$ symmetric convex bodies in $\R^n$, then for all $0 \leq t \leq 1$ and $p\geq 0$ $$ |tK +_p (1-t)L| \geq |K|^t |L|^{1-t}. $$
If $K$ and $L$ are convex bodies that contain the origin in their interiors then the $L_p$-combination $tK +_p (1-t)L$ is defined by $$ tK +_p (1-t)L = \underset{u \in S^{n-1}}{\cap} \left\{ x \in \R^n:\ \left < x , u \right> \leq \left(t h_K(u)^p + (1-t) h_L(u)^p \right)^{\frac1p} \right\}. $$
Inequalities
Symmetry and convexity in geometric inequalities
The intended claim is an L_p-Brunn-Minkowski inequality for symmetric convex bodies, including p=0.

aimpl_batch.text_excerpt: Log-Brunn-Minkowski Inequality Show that if $K$ and $L$ symmetric convex bodies in $\R^n$, then for all $0 \leq t \leq 1$ the following hods $$ |tK +_\circ (1-t)L| \geq |K|^t |L|^{1-t} $$ with equality if and only if $K = L$ or $K$ and $L$ are parallelograms with parallel sides. For convex bodies $K$ and $L$ in $\R^n$ with support functions $h_K$ and $h_L$ the logarithmic sum $tK +_\circ (1-t)L$ is defined as $$ tK +_\circ (1-t)L = \underset{u \in S^{n-1}}{\cap} \left\{x \in \R^n:\ \langle x, u\rangle \leq h_K(u)^th_L(u)^{1-t} \right\} $$ where $h_K(u) = \max\limits_{x \in K} \langle x, u\rangle .$ Inequalities Symmetry and convexity in geometric inequalities The intended claim is the origin-symmetric log-Brunn-Minkowski inequality.

conjecturebench.label: Log-Brunn–Minkowski conjecture
conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Log-Brunn–Minkowski conjecture Log-Brunn–Minkowski conjecture · 2012. For origin-symmetric convex bodies \(K,L\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(0\le\lambda\le1\), it asserts \(V((1-\lambda)\cdot K+_0\lambda\cdot L)\ge V(K)^{1-\lambda}V(L)^\lambda\), where the log-sum is the Wulff body with support datum \(h_K^{1-\lambda}h_L^\lambda\) (original).

oeis.label: A092374

For convex bodies $K$ and $L$ in $\R^n$ with support functions $h_K$ and $h_L$ the logarithmic sum $tK +_\circ (1-t)L$ is defined as $$ tK +_\circ (1-t)L = \underset{u \in S^{n-1}}{\cap} \left\{x \in \R^n:\ \langle x, u\rangle \leq h_K(u)^th_L(u)^{1-t} \right\} $$ where $h_K(u) = \max\limits_{x \in K} \langle x, u\rangle .$ Inequalities Symmetry and convexity in geometric inequalities The intended claim is the origin-symmetric log-Brunn-Minkowski inequality.

For \(0\le\mu_1\le\cdots\le\mu_n\) with \(\sum_i\mu_i<1\), it predicts that over independent nonnegative \(X_i\) with \(E X_i=\mu_i\), \(\inf P(\sum_iX_i<1)=\min_{0\le t<n}\prod_{i=t+1}^n\left(1-\frac{\mu_i}{1-\sum_{j=1}^t\mu_j}\right)\) (original).

query_text:
$L^1$ norm of first eigenfunction.
Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be an open set with finite measure, $\lambda_1(\Omega)$ be the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian with Dirichlet boundary conditions, and let \[T(\Omega)=\int_{\Omega}u\] where $u:\Omega\to \mathbb{R}$ is the torsion function given by the equation \[\begin{cases} -\Delta u=1 & \text{ in }\Omega\\ u=0 & \text{ in }\partial\Omega \end{cases}\] Let $F(\Omega) = \lambda_1(\Omega)T(\Omega)/|\Omega|$. Then it is known that $F(\Omega)$ is bounded between $0$ and $1$, and these bounds are sharp. However when one restricts to convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$, there is a better bound \[\frac{\pi^2}{32}\leq F(\Omega)\leq 0.9967\] The left-hand side is due to [Brasco, Mazzoleni], and the right-hand side to [Ftouhi]. The conjecture raised by Phanuel Mariano is as follows: for any planar convex set $\Omega$, does one has \[\frac{\pi^2}{24}\leq F(\Omega)\leq \frac{\pi^2}{12}\] If these bounds were verified, they would be sharp in the following sense: the right one is asymptotically reached for thin rectangles, while the left one is asymptotically reached for any sequence of triangles that collapses on the interval. More recently in [Banuelos, Mariano], these bounds were proven in the case where $\Omega$ is either a triangle or a rectangle.
Eigenfunctions
Symmetry-breaking of optimal shapes
A question asking for sharp lower and upper bounds on lambda_1 times torsional rigidity for planar convex sets.

conjecturebench.label: Log-Brunn–Minkowski conjecture
conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Log-Brunn–Minkowski conjecture Log-Brunn–Minkowski conjecture · 2012. For origin-symmetric convex bodies \(K,L\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(0\le\lambda\le1\), it asserts \(V((1-\lambda)\cdot K+_0\lambda\cdot L)\ge V(K)^{1-\lambda}V(L)^\lambda\), where the log-sum is the Wulff body with support datum \(h_K^{1-\lambda}h_L^\lambda\) (original).

conjecturebench.label: Compatible triangulations
conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Compatible triangulations Any two general-position planar n-point sets with equal convex-hull size have combinatorially compatible triangulations.

conjecturebench.label: Independent arborescences on convex sets in acyclic digraphs
conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Independent arborescences on convex sets in acyclic digraphs Let D=(V,A) be an acyclic digraph, let r_1,...,r_k be designated roots, and let U_1,...,U_k be convex vertex sets with r_i in U_i. If, for every v, the paths r_i-to-v for all i with v in U_i can be chosen pairwise openly node-disjoint, then there are independent r_i-arborescences F_i with V(F_i)=U_i.

conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Wegner’s planar graph-square conjecture Wegner’s planar graph-square conjecture · 1977. Its Δ=4 case predicts that the square of every planar graph is 9-colorable.

conjecturebench.label: Negami planar-cover conjecture
conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Negami planar-cover conjecture A connected graph has a finite planar cover if and only if it embeds in the projective plane.

conjecturebench.label: Reed’s ω–Δ–χ conjecture
conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Reed’s ω–Δ–χ conjecture Reed’s ω–Δ–χ conjecture · formulated around 1995 and published in 1998. Every graph satisfies \(\chi\le\lceil(\Delta+1+\omega)/2\rceil\).

conjecturebench.label: Dürer–Shephard edge-unfolding conjecture
conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Dürer–Shephard edge-unfolding conjecture Every convex polyhedron has a nonoverlapping planar unfolding obtained by cutting a spanning tree of its edges.

conjecturebench.label: Marcus–de Oliveira determinantal conjecture
conjecturebench.text_excerpt: Marcus–de Oliveira determinantal conjecture Marcus–de Oliveira determinantal conjecture · 1973/1982. For normal \(A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\), \(\det(A+B)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{co}\{\prod_{j=1}^n(\lambda_j(A)+\lambda_{\sigma(j)}(B)):\sigma\in S_n\}\). Marcus posed it in 1973 and de Oliveira independently in 1982 (survey).

oeis.label: A008486
oeis.text_excerpt: The conjecture is correct. Proof: For n=0 the theorem holds, the maximum planar graph has n+2=2 vertices and 1 edge. Now suppose that we have a connected planar graph with at least 3 vertices. If it contains a face that is not a triangle, we can add an edge that divides this face into two without breaking its planarity. Hence all maximum planar graphs are triangulations. Euler's formula for planar graphs states that in any planar simple graph with V vertices, E edges and F faces we have V+F-E=2. If all faces are triangles, then F=2E/3, which gives us E=3V-6. Hence for n>0 each maximum planar simple graph with n+2 vertices has 3n edges. - _Michal Forisek_, Apr 23 2009

oeis.label: A356851
oeis.text_excerpt: For n > 250 the terms are concentrated along seven lines, see the linked images. Unlike the other six lines, numbers along the second lowest line are somewhat spread out, and these terms contain all numbers with Omega(a(n)) > 1. The lowest line contains all the primes, while the upper five lines contain terms with Omega(a(n)) = 2, 3, and 4. The primes up to n=100000 occur in their natural order except for 11 and 13 which are switched. The only fixed point beyond the first two terms is 10, and it is likely no more exist. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers.

oeis.label: A010815
oeis.text_excerpt: The conjecture is correct: By Euler's Pentagonal Number Theorem, the sum equals Product_{k >= 1} (1 - exp(-Pi*k)) = eta(i/2)*exp(Pi/24), where eta(t) = q^(1/24) * Product_{n >= 1} (1 - q^n), q = exp(2*Pi*i*t), is Dedekind's eta fumction. The conjecture follows from the standard result that eta(i/2) = Gamma(1/4)/(2^(7/8)*Pi^(3/4)) (see, for example, the Wikipedia entry on the eta function) and the reflection formula for the Gamma function. - _Peter Bala_, May 22 2026
